Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the ShopSphere Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to ShopSphere Inc.'s Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Jamie Chen, CEO; Taylor Brooks, CFO; and Morgan Patel, COO.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call may contain forward-looking statements, including our expectations for future financial performance, business strategies, and market trends. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete list of these risks and uncertainties.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Jamie Chen, CEO of ShopSphere Inc.

Jamie Chen:
Thank you, Alex, and good afternoon, everyone. We are pleased to report a strong Q3 performance, driven by evolving customer purchasing habits that boosted order frequency, and our ability to navigate macroeconomic headwinds impacting GMV and revenue.

Our focus remains on enhancing efficiency in managing operating costs. We are also excited about the initial traction we are seeing with our NextBuy AI engine and ShopSphere Prime loyalty program, which we believe will significantly drive higher engagement and repeat business across categories.

Finally, we are committed to analyzing and mitigating seasonality impacts through data-driven forecasting and evergreen revenue streams.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Taylor Brooks, our CFO, to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Taylor Brooks:
Thank you, Jamie. Our Q3 revenue was $2.9 billion, an increase of 11% year-over-year. Gross margin was 39.2%, driven by improved take rates from advertising and subscriptions, as well as optimized fulfillment efficiencies. Operating expenses were $650 million, representing 22.4% of revenue, reflecting strong cost discipline across all lines.

Our net income for the quarter was $265 million, or $0.88 per share. We ended the quarter with $4.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are reaffirming our full-year guidance of $11.8 to $12.2 billion in revenue and 12-14% GMV growth.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deep into one of our key engagement metrics: order frequency, which we define as the average number of orders placed per active customer over the trailing 12 months. This metric is a cornerstone of our flywheel in the e-commerce space, directly fueling lifetime value, or LTV, while complementing average order value, or AOV, and cohort retention rates. In Q3, our order frequency reached 4.2 orders per active customer, marking a robust 15% year-over-year increase from 3.65 in the prior year. This not only outpaced the broader online retail industry's average of around 3.1—per recent eMarketer data—but also positions us ahead of peers like Stitch Fix at 3.8 and Wayfair at 3.4.

Let me unpack the drivers behind this shift in customer purchasing habits, which reflect a broader secular trend toward more habitual, convenience-driven shopping in e-commerce. Post-pandemic, we've seen consumers evolve from episodic big-ticket purchases—think quarterly hauls during Prime Day equivalents—to higher-frequency, lower-AOV micro-transactions. Our data shows weekly order frequency among our active user base surging from 20% to 35% year-over-year, with the median basket size for these impulse buys dipping to $28, down 8% but more than offset by the sheer volume. This mirrors patterns at Amazon, where their Subscribe & Save model has trained over 200 million customers into routine replenishment, but we're capturing it across a multi-category marketplace spanning fashion, consumer electronics, beauty, and home goods.

Cohort analysis tells an even more compelling story. New customers acquired in Q3 averaged 1.8 orders in their first 90 days, up from 1.4 last year—a testament to our onboarding funnel. Meanwhile, our two-year vintage cohort is humming at 7.1 orders annually, with churn compressing to 18% from 24%. Subscription penetration is the rocket fuel here: subscriptions now represent 25% of our active customer base, driving 42% of all repeat orders and boosting frequency by an incremental 1.2 orders per subscriber. Our SphereLoop auto-replenishment program—similar to Instacart's model but integrated natively into our app—has seen adoption skyrocket 60% year-over-year, particularly for fast-moving categories like skincare, such as CeraVe serums, and pantry staples via our expanded Ulta Beauty partnership.

Regionally, the picture is nuanced, reflecting macroeconomic tailwinds and our tailored strategies. North America, 55% of GMV, saw frequency hold steady at 4.0, pressured by inflation-weary consumers trading down on non-essentials. However, our urban millennials—core to 40% of orders—are leaning into social commerce, with TikTok Shop integrations lifting frequency 22% among 18-34s via shoppable short-form videos. Europe, 25% of GMV, was a standout at 4.8 orders per customer, up 18% year-over-year, fueled by our aggressive localization post-Brexit. In the UK and Germany, GDPR-compliant personalization has resonated, with ASOS-inspired outfit builders increasing fashion repeat rates by 30%. We're also capitalizing on the EU's Digital Markets Act by prioritizing first-party data. APAC, 15% of GMV and growing fastest, exploded to 5.6 orders, a 28% year-over-year jump, driven by Southeast Asia's super-app habits akin to Shopee and Lazada. In India, our JioMart tie-up has embedded us in daily grocery rituals, pushing frequency among lower-funnel users to weekly norms. Rest of World, 5%, is emerging at 3.9, with LatAm pilots showing early promise through Mercado Libre-style installments.

Technically, we've supercharged this with our NextBuy AI engine, a proprietary recommendation system leveraging LLM-powered behavioral clustering on 1.2 billion historical sessions. This has improved next-purchase prediction accuracy to 42%, up from 32%, delivering personalized nudges via push notifications and in-app carousels—think "Your weekly tech refresh: AirPods Pro at 15% off." We've also rolled out ShopSphere Prime, our loyalty tier with free next-day delivery on orders over $15, which has lifted frequency 25% among enrollees by reducing friction. Under the hood, our Shopify Plus backbone handles a 3x spike in micro-orders without latency, while Snowflake data warehousing enables real-time cohort scoring.

Strategically, these habit shifts are accretive to our ARPU, which climbed 12% to $156, and position us for LTV expansion to $650 over three years. We're not complacent—in Q4, we'll pilot AR try-on for beauty in partnership with L'Oréal, targeting a 20% frequency uplift in that $10 billion category. Amid softening consumer sentiment, with U.S. retail sales growth at just 2.5% per Census Bureau, we're doubling down on value stacking: bundling with DoorDash for same-hour fulfillment and launching Frequency Rewards credits redeemable across 500+ brands.

Looking ahead, we guide for full-year order frequency of 4.3, with mid-teens growth into FY25 as AI maturity and APAC scale compound. This isn't just about more orders—it's rewiring habits for sustained dominance in a $6.5 trillion global e-commerce market, projected by Statista to grow at 10% CAGR through 2027.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for ShopSphere Inc. Today, I'd like to dive deep into our operating expenses, where we've made significant strides in efficiency, delivering a 420 basis point improvement in our OpEx as a percentage of net revenue, now standing at 22.3% compared to 26.5% in Q3 last year. This reflects not just cost discipline but proactive strategies tailored to the e-commerce sector's unique pressures—rising logistics inflation, competitive marketing battles, and the need for scalable tech infrastructure amid softening consumer demand in certain categories like apparel and electronics.

Let me break this down by key line items, highlighting the trends, initiatives, and regional nuances that underpinned our $650 million in total OpEx for the quarter, down 4% year-over-year on a constant currency basis, even as GMV grew 8% to $16.5 billion.

Fulfillment costs remain our largest OpEx bucket at 42% of the total, or $273 million in Q3, but we achieved an 11% year-over-year decline on an absolute basis and a sharp 180 basis point contraction to 9.8% of net revenue. This efficiency stems from our SmartFulfill network expansion, where we've deployed over 150 micro-fulfillment centers globally, mimicking Amazon's hub-and-spoke model but with a twist: AI-powered dynamic routing that reduced last-mile delivery costs by 22% per package.

Key trends here include normalizing parcel volumes post-pandemic—our average packages per order stabilized at 1.8, down from 2.1 in 2022—and aggressive carrier negotiations. We locked in volume-based discounts with FedEx and DHL, yielding a blended shipping rate of $4.72 per unit, 15% below industry averages per ShipBob benchmarks. Regionally, North America drove 60% of savings through robotics adoption in our Texas and California DCs, where Kiva-style autonomous mobile robots handled 65% of picks, slashing labor costs by 28%. In APAC, particularly India and Southeast Asia, where labor is cheaper but infrastructure lags, we partnered with local players like Delhivery to cut fulfillment times to under 24 hours, boosting NPS by 12 points while holding costs flat at 8.5% of GMV. Europe faced headwinds from the EU's ETS carbon taxes, but our shift to electric last-mile fleets with Rivian vans reduced costs by 9% year-over-year.

Marketing and sales expenses came in at $312 million, or 6.5% of net revenue—down 150 basis points year-over-year and 14% below plan. Customer Acquisition Cost, or CAC, improved to $28 per new active customer, a 17% reduction, driven by our ML-enhanced personalization engine. We're leveraging first-party data from our 250 million global users to serve hyper-targeted ads, achieving a 3.2x ROAS on platforms like Meta and Google, outperforming Shopify merchants' average of 2.5x.

Strategically, we've de-emphasized broad performance marketing in favor of loyalty loops—our Prime-like ShopSphere Plus subscription now at 45% penetration grew retention by 18%, amortizing CAC payback to under 4 months. In LATAM, where economic volatility hit impulse buys, we pivoted to shoppable TikTok Lives and Instagram Reels, cutting CAC by 25% in Brazil and Mexico amid a 20% regional GMV uptick. This contrasts with mature markets like the UK, where privacy regs like GDPR forced a 10% reallocation to owned channels, yet still yielded efficiency gains.

Technology and content OpEx totaled $210 million, flat year-over-year but 90 basis points more efficient at 4.4% of revenue. We've optimized AWS spend via reserved instances and spot pricing, saving $45 million annualized—similar to how Etsy scaled back on underutilized EC2 fleets. Our proprietary NovaAI platform, now processing 10 petabytes daily, uses predictive inventory algorithms to reduce stockouts by 35% and overstock markdowns from 12% to 7% of inventory value.

Initiatives like serverless architecture on Lambda cut compute costs 40%, while GenAI tools automate 70% of product descriptions, freeing content teams for high-value SEO. In China, mirroring Alibaba's playbook, we integrated with WeChat Mini-Programs, boosting mobile conversion 22% without proportional tech uplift.

General and administrative expenses held steady at $174 million, or 3.6% of revenue, with headcount flat at 28,000 despite GMV growth. Remote-first policies and offshore shared services in the Philippines trimmed overhead by 8%, aligning with peers like Wayfair.

Looking ahead, we expect OpEx margins to compress another 100-150 basis points in the second half through sustainability plays—like our $100 million investment in zero-emission warehouses, targeting Scope 3 reductions that could unlock 5-7% logistics savings by 2025—and deeper vertical integration, including private-label expansions in beauty and groceries à la Instacart. Risks include FX volatility in emerging markets and potential tariff hikes on China imports, but our 65/35 domestic/international sourcing mix mitigates this.

In summary, these efficiencies generated $280 million in incremental Adjusted EBITDA, pushing our margin to 14.2%—top quartile versus e-commerce peers. We're not just cutting costs; we're building a resilient, tech-forward machine for the next wave of growth.

Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q3 2024 earnings call. As we dive into our financial results, I'd like to spend some time addressing the impact of macroeconomic factors on our Gross Merchandise Value, or GMV, and revenue. This has been a pivotal quarter where resilience met headwinds, and our performance underscores the unique dynamics of the E-Commerce ecosystem.

To set the stage: Q3 GMV came in at $16.5 billion, up 8% year-over-year, reflecting persistent macro pressures. Revenue reached $2.9 billion, a solid 11% increase, driven by a 2.5 percentage point expansion in our take rate to 17.5%, reflecting higher monetization from advertising and our ShopSphere Plus subscription fees. Active buyers grew 5% to 190 million, with repeat purchase rates holding steady at 68%, but AOV dipped 1% to $87 amid softer discretionary spending.

Let's break down the key macroeconomic influences, starting with inflation and consumer spending patterns. Headline CPI inflation averaged 3.2% globally in Q3, per IMF data, squeezing household budgets and shifting demand toward value-oriented categories. Discretionary segments like apparel and consumer electronics, which represent 45% of our GMV, saw a 10% year-over-year decline in units sold, with ASPs down 6% due to aggressive promotions—our promotional discount rate rose to 26% from 22% last year. This mirrors trends at peers like Etsy and Wayfair, where comparable softness hit mid-teens. Conversely, essentials like groceries and household supplies surged 16% in GMV, benefiting from our same-day delivery partnerships with Instacart-like services and our private-label Essentials by ShopSphere line, which captured 15% market share in that vertical.

Interest rates played a significant role too. The Fed's terminal rate at 5.25-5.50% and ECB's parallel hikes to 4% curbed credit availability, particularly impacting Buy Now Pay Later, or BNPL, penetration. Our BNPL GMV mix fell from 22% to 18%, echoing Affirm's reported 15% volume drop. This shaved roughly 3 percentage points off our overall AOV growth, as higher-income cohorts deferred big-ticket items like appliances. However, we mitigated this through targeted financing with Klarna integrations, maintaining BNPL authorization rates above 85%.

Currency headwinds were acute in international markets. A 7% USD appreciation against a basket of EM currencies pressured APAC and LatAm GMV by 5% on a constant-currency basis. In Brazil, where we derive 12% of total GMV via our Mercado Libre-inspired marketplace model, the real's 10% depreciation led to a 14% FX hit, partially offset by 20% local-currency growth from hyper-localized assortments in beauty and fashion.

Regionally: North America, 55% of GMV, up 5% year-over-year to $9.1 billion. Elevated unemployment claims—up 8% per BLS data—dampened middle-market spending, but urban millennials drove 12% growth in mobile commerce, now 62% of orders. Our AI-driven dynamic pricing engine, powered by similar tech to Amazon's, adjusted 1.2 million SKUs in real-time, preserving margins amid 5% input cost inflation from Red Sea disruptions. Europe, 25% of GMV, up 2% at $4.1 billion. Energy prices lingering 15% above pre-Ukraine levels fueled an 8% drop in home goods, akin to Zalando's guidance. We countered with Flash Deals campaigns, boosting conversion rates 7% via our SAP Commerce Cloud platform. APAC, 15% of GMV, up 3% to $2.5 billion, hit by China's property slump and India's monsoon delays. TikTok Shop-like short-video integrations lifted Southeast Asia GMV 25%, with Indonesia up 30% on gamified loyalty rewards. LatAm & Other, 5% of GMV, robust 14% growth to $820 million, resilient despite Argentina's 200%+ inflation, thanks to dollar-denominated pricing and Rappi-style quick commerce.

Geopolitical factors amplified supply chain volatility. Ongoing Red Sea tensions inflated ocean freight rates 40% year-over-year, per Drewry Index, delaying 20% of our China-sourced inventory—primarily electronics and toys. This contributed to a 150 basis point inventory turnover slowdown to 8.2x. We've responded with technical initiatives like our Supplier Risk AI model, which rerouted 65% of shipments via Vietnam and Mexico, reducing lead times 22% and mirroring Shein’s nearshoring playbook.

On revenue specifically, macro pressures compressed GMV but we leaned into marketplace economics. Fulfillment fees, 42% of revenue, grew 12% as AOV compression was offset by higher units per order from bundling algorithms. Advertising revenue exploded 24% to $680 million, fueled by Sponsored Products akin to Amazon's, with ROAS for advertisers averaging 4.5x amid 30% more search queries for deals and discounts. ShopSphere Plus, our $139/year subscription, hit 48 million members—up 18%—driving 35% higher LTV and shielding 22% of GMV from promotions.

Strategically, we're positioning for a soft-landing scenario. We've launched Value Vault, a private-label assortment with 2,000 SKUs at 20-30% below competitors, targeting inflation-weary Gen Z—early traction shows 40% repeat rates. Technologically, our GenAI recommendation engine, processing 10 billion daily signals, improved basket size 5% by cross-selling essentials with discretionary upsells. We're also diversifying into social commerce, partnering with Meta for shoppable Instagram Reels, projecting 10% incremental GMV in the second half.

Looking ahead, we see Q4 GMV growth of 8-10%, assuming CPI eases to 2.8% and no recession. Downside risks include prolonged high rates or China stimulus shortfalls; upsides from potential Fed cuts could unlock 13%+ growth. Our $4.5 billion cash pile funds $1.2 billion in share buybacks and capex for micro-fulfillment centers, ensuring we outpace industry peers like Shopify merchants, guiding 6-8% GMV, and Pinduoduo's Temu, facing U.S. tariff scrutiny.

In summary, macros dented top-line momentum, but our asset-light model, data moat, and customer-centric innovations delivered resilient results.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. As we dive into the financials, I'd like to spend some time on seasonality, a core dynamic in our e-commerce model that drives both opportunities and challenges. ShopSphere, as a leading multi-category online retailer with over $60 billion in annual GMV, experiences pronounced seasonal patterns tied to consumer spending cycles, promotional events, and macroeconomic factors. Today, I'll analyze historical and current trends, explain key deviations from our expectations, and outline our strategic responses, including technical initiatives and regional nuances.

First, let's set the baseline with historical trends. Over the past five years, our revenue has followed a classic e-commerce seasonality profile: Q4 accounting for 42-48% of full-year revenue, driven by Black Friday/Cyber Monday, or BFCM, which in 2023 generated $3.2 billion in GMV—a 25% year-over-year increase—and contributed 15% of annual sales in just five days. Q1 softens to 18-20% of annual revenue post-holiday fatigue, Q2 sees a modest lift from back-to-school and summer sales around 22%, and Q3 ramps up with early holiday prep, typically 20-22%. This mirrors industry peers like Amazon and Shopify merchants, where Adobe Analytics data shows U.S. e-commerce sales spiking 150-200% during peak holiday weeks.

Key metrics underscore this: AOV surges 25-35% in Q4 to $85-95 from a baseline of $65, fueled by bundling and upsell algorithms. Conversion rates climb from 3.2% annually to 5.8% during BFCM, while traffic volumes double via paid search and social ads. However, CAC balloons 40-50% in peak periods due to bidding wars on Google Ads and Meta platforms, partially offset by higher LTV from repeat purchases—our Q4 cohorts show 2.5x LTV payback within 12 months versus 18 months for off-peak.

Turning to Q3 2024 trends, we delivered solid results with $2.9 billion in revenue, up 11% year-over-year, but seasonality played out as expected with GMV growth of 8% versus our guided 10-12%. Halloween and early Black Friday prep drove a 20% AOV increase to $78, supported by our Trick-or-Treat Deals campaign, which mirrored Etsy’s success in niche gifting. Mobile commerce, now 62% of orders, amplified this—our app-exclusive flash sales converted at 6.1%, up from 4.8% last year.

Now, deviations: We saw a 2-point underperformance in Q3 GMV growth, primarily from two factors. First, softer U.S. demand in apparel and electronics—categories representing 35% of our mix—due to inventory overhang from Q2 supply chain easing. U.S. GMV grew 6% year-over-year versus 10% expected, with AOV flat at $72 amid consumer pullback on discretionary spend, echoing Walmart's recent comps amid 3.7% CPI inflation. Second, a positive deviation in non-peak categories: Home & Garden surged 26% year-over-year to $480 million GMV, bucking the trend thanks to our pivot to subscription models like ShopSphere Home Essentials, which now has 1.2 million subscribers generating $190 million in recurring revenue—up 42% year-over-year and reducing seasonality exposure by 8% year-over-year.

Regionally, patterns diverged sharply. In North America, 65% of revenue, seasonality intensified with BFCM hype, but early Halloween sales dipped 4% due to warm weather impacting seasonal decor—think less demand for pumpkins in a La Niña year. Europe, 20% of revenue, outperformed with 17% GMV growth, propelled by Singles' Day spillover from APAC partners and our localized Black Friday launches ahead of VAT season; AOV hit €82, 12% above trend, via dynamic pricing tied to GBP/EUR fluctuations. APAC, 15% of revenue, our fastest-growing region, showed muted Q3 at 10% growth versus 14% expected—Chinese Golden Week underdelivered amid zero-COVID unwind and real estate woes, but India’s festive season, Diwali, boosted 24% with 1.5 million new users via Flipkart integrations.

These deviations aren't anomalies; they're structural shifts. Macro headwinds like rising interest rates, Fed funds at 5.25-5.50%, compressed consumer wallets, per Nielsen data showing 7% drop in discretionary e-comm spend. Yet, we mitigated via technical initiatives: Our AI-powered demand forecasting engine, built on AWS SageMaker and processing 10 billion SKUs daily, improved inventory turns by 22%—reducing stockouts from 12% to 4% during peaks and enabling just-in-time replenishment with suppliers like Shein and Temu. We rolled out Seasonal Surge ML, a proprietary model using Prophet time-series forecasting integrated with Google Cloud BigQuery, which predicted BFCM traffic with 92% accuracy, up from 85% last year. This allowed hyper-personalized recommendations via our NovaAI engine, lifting cross-sell rates 18% and adding $160 million in incremental GMV.

Strategically, we're de-risking seasonality. We've doubled down on evergreen categories: Groceries via same-day delivery partnerships with Instacart now contribute 12% of GMV, up from 5%, with 65% gross margins versus 45% for fashion. Subscription ARPU grew 32% to $45/month, smoothing cash flows—our forward guidance assumes subscriptions hit 20% of revenue by FY2025. Internationally, we're launching ShopSphereFest in APAC for Lunar New Year, targeting 25% GMV uplift, while in Europe, GDPR-compliant data lakes enable 15% better retention via loyalty programs akin to Zalando Plus.

Looking ahead, Q4 guidance reflects tempered seasonality: $5.0-5.2 billion revenue, 12-14% GMV growth, with BFCM at $3.4 billion. Deviations could arise from shipping rates, down 10% post-peak Red Sea disruptions, or tariff risks, but our 40% owned-fulfillment network positions us well. We're confident in navigating this, much like Shopify's 2023 playbook during inflation.

Operator, we are now ready for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time we will begin the question and answer session. [Operator instructions for Q&A session]. Our first question comes from Sarah Lin with Morgan Stanley.

Sarah Lin:
Thanks for taking my question. Taylor, your commentary on order frequency was impressive, especially the regional breakdowns and AI contributions. Can you elaborate on how SphereLoop is performing in APAC and any risks to sustaining that 28% growth there?

Jamie Chen:
Thanks, Sarah. SphereLoop has been a game-changer in APAC, particularly with super-app integrations mirroring Shopee, where daily grocery habits are embedding it deeply. Adoption is up 60% year-over-year, driving that explosive 5.6 orders per customer. Risks like FX volatility exist, but our local partnerships with JioMart mitigate them, and we're guiding mid-teens growth into next year.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with Goldman Sachs.

David Patel:
Great, thanks. Taylor, on the macro impacts, with BNPL softening, how are you thinking about financing options long-term, and what's the outlook for ad revenue amid search shifts to deals?

Taylor Brooks:
David, spot on. BNPL dipped to 18% mix due to rates, but Klarna keeps approvals high. Long-term, we're expanding in-house financing for stability. Ads grew 24% on deal queries, 4.5x ROAS, and we expect continued strength as Value Vault private labels draw more advertiser spend in H2.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with JPMorgan.

Emily Chen:
Thank you. Impressive OpEx leverage—can the COO comment on fulfillment network scalability for Q4 seasonality, especially with Red Sea ongoing?

Morgan Patel:
Emily, thanks. Our 150+ SmartFulfill centers with AI routing are scaled for Q4 peaks, handling 3x volume spikes like last BFCM. Red Sea rerouting via Vietnam cut lead times 22%, and robotics in NA DCs keep costs down 28%. We're on track for 100-150 bps further compression.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the call back over to Jamie Chen for closing remarks.

Jamie Chen:
Thank you for joining us today. We are confident in our ability to continue to execute our strategy and deliver long-term value for our shareholders. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
